claims.text: An intermetallic or ceramic matrix can be tailored to produce a wide-temperature self-lubricating composite.
Precipitating high-temperature-stable lubricious phases can balance mechanical strength and self-lubricating performance.
The initial intermetallic or ceramic material has high mechanical strength.
The initial material lacks intrinsic high-temperature lubrication functionality.
Introducing suitable alloying elements and applying controlled processing can form stable lubricious precipitates within the matrix.
The intervention produces a dispersed, stable secondary lubricious phase within the primary structural matrix.
The precipitated lubricious phases provide low-shear interfaces.
Low-shear interfaces formed by the precipitates facilitate self-lubrication and reduce friction and wear.
The continuous matrix maintains the composite's structural integrity while the secondary phase provides lubrication.
The modified composite will have a lower friction coefficient than an unmodified material at moderate and very high temperatures.
The modified composite will have a lower wear rate than an unmodified material at moderate and very high temperatures.
The lubrication improvement will occur without compromising mechanical strength.
Mechanically robust unmodified intermetallic or ceramic materials lacking built-in lubrication have higher friction at high temperatures.
Mechanically robust unmodified intermetallic or ceramic materials lacking built-in lubrication experience accelerated wear at high temperatures.
Nonuniform precipitate distribution can prevent the intended balance between strength and lubrication.
Loss of precipitate stability during cyclic high-temperature exposure can prevent the intended balance between strength and lubrication.
